summary: Mike Padlipsky offers two solutions to the problem, raised in RFC 487, of sending a file to someone without knowing their password. One adds a convention so the recipient pulls the file, the other adds a command. They avoid the objections to a daemon approach raised in RFC 501.

plainLanguage.summary: This note considers how to deliver a file when the sender does not know the recipient's password. The recipient can retrieve the file, or a server can hold it in a pool for later pickup.

subtitle: Two proposals for sending a file without knowing the recipient's password.

tldr.problem: A sender may want to give another user a file without knowing that user's password, while direct access to the recipient's directory raises access-control concerns.
tldr.mechanism: The recipient can retrieve a file using their own credentials, or the sender can place it in a pool directory and notify the recipient.
tldr.outcome: The author proposes a new FTP POOL command for the second approach and asks for comments on access-control needs.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 505 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. The POOL command is presented as a proposal for FTP.

sections.title: The Access Problem
sections.content: RFC 505 responds to a question about sending a file to a user on another system without knowing that user's password. It also considers objections to having a daemon process perform the transfer using a separate access-control scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender needs to deliver a file but should not need the recipient's password. The note considers ways to avoid granting broad access to the recipient's directory.

sections.title: Letting the Recipient Retrieve the File
sections.content:
One approach reverses the transfer: the sender grants suitable access to the file, and the recipient uses their own identity and User FTP to retrieve it from the sender's Server FTP.

This requires the recipient to have an account on the sender's system or access to a known free Server FTP account, and the recipient must be able to start the transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipient can log in with their own credentials and pull the file. This works only if they can access the sender's server.

sections.title: The Proposed POOL Command
sections.content:
The other approach stores the incoming file in a pool directory instead of placing it directly in the recipient's directory. The server notifies the named recipient, who can copy the file into their own directory if they want it.

The proposed POOL command takes a recipient identifier and file name. The server should validate the identifier and make the pooled name unique.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can hold the file in a separate area and tell the recipient it is there. The recipient decides whether to copy it into their own directory.
